findings.message: The PR changes plugin code (new `show` and `fields` subcommands in specclaw-sync, a new plugin, and a specclaw test edit) but shows no version bump on any existing plugin. All plugins must share one version. If this is a release, every `plugin.json` (claude and codex) and every `marketplace.json` entry must move together; the new plugin is at 0.8.7 and specclaw-sync is not bumped in this diff.
findings.scenario: specclaw-sync gains new subcommands but its `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` versions are untouched. Users on the old version never receive `fields`/`show`, and fleet's `record` calls fail against the cached older plugin.

findings.message: The namespace enforces `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`, but the Job pod sets no `seccompProfile` (RuntimeDefault) at pod or container level. The restricted profile requires one. The API server rejects the pods, and the Job sits with FailedCreate events. Add `seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}` to the pod securityContext.
findings.scenario: `specclaw-fleet dispatch` creates the Job and Secret, and the work item is set to Dispatched. The Job controller cannot create the pod (violates PodSecurity restricted), so the work item stays Dispatched forever and nothing runs.

findings.message: The squid Deployment is applied into the `restricted` namespace with no securityContext: no runAsNonRoot, no allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, no capabilities drop and no seccompProfile. `ubuntu/squid` also normally starts as root. Admission rejects the pod, so there is no egress proxy and every fleet pod loses all connectivity. Set a non-root user, drop all capabilities, set seccomp RuntimeDefault, and make the paths squid writes to (logs, pid, cache) writable for that user.
findings.scenario: `kubectl apply -f k8s/` creates the Deployment, but its ReplicaSet cannot create pods (PodSecurity violation). `fleet-egress` has no endpoints and agents fail at clone/API calls.

findings.message: `az keyvault secret show ... || az keyvault secret set ... --value __unset__` treats any `show` failure (throttle, network error, missing get permission, expired login) as 'secret does not exist'. It then overwrites a user's real registered credential with the placeholder. Only create the secret when the failure is specifically NotFound; otherwise die.
findings.scenario: Alice has a registered claude token. An admin re-runs `onboard alice@x.com` while `az keyvault secret show` fails transiently. The script runs `secret set --value __unset__` and Alice's token is destroyed.

findings.message: `fetch_credential` returns 1 both for 'no credential registered' (absent or `__unset__`) and for 'could not ask the vault' (az not logged in, network, 403). `check_gates` reports both as 'assignee has no registered credential' and marks the work item Failed with that reason. Distinguish a vault read error from not-found and surface it as an error, not as the assignee's problem.
findings.scenario: The pipeline's `az` session lacks vault read access, or the vault is briefly unreachable. Every dispatch is refused, each work item is set to Failed with 'run specclaw-fleet login', and the assignee re-registers a token that was fine.

findings.message: The doc and header promise that `fields` 'always posts one comment' so the record survives. But the field PATCH runs first and `die`s on failure, so the comment is never posted. An invalid state transition or a bad field reference loses the whole record. Post the comment before the PATCH, or post it even when the PATCH fails.
findings.scenario: `azdo.fleet_states.failed: Failed` is mapped, but the work item is in a state that cannot move to Failed. The PATCH returns 400, `die` fires, and no comment is posted. The entrypoint only prints a warning, so the run record is lost.

findings.message: Write-back uploads `auth.json` whenever its hash differs from the seed. It does not check that the file is valid JSON or non-empty. A truncated or corrupted file overwrites the assignee's working credential in the vault. Validate with `jq -e .` (and that it still has the expected token fields) before the PUT, and otherwise keep the old secret and report.
findings.scenario: codex leaves `auth.json` as `{` or garbage (killed mid-write, or steered by prompt injection). The hash differs from the seed, writeback PUTs it, and the next dispatch for that user fails authentication until they re-login.

findings.message: The 'one codex job per person' guarantee is a check-then-create (`codex_busy` then `launch_job`) with no atomic claim. README admits both can pass, yet the same README states the limit as a guarantee for safety reasons. The test (ac6) is single-session. Use an atomic claim, for example a per-assignee object created with `kubectl create` that fails if it already exists, and add a two-worker race test.
findings.scenario: Two commits flip two proposals to approved for the same assignee, so two pipeline runs start in parallel. Both see no active codex Job and both launch. The same rotating `auth.json` is used concurrently and one refresh token is invalidated.

findings.message: Agent stdout and stderr go only to `$STATUS/agent.log` on an emptyDir. It is not printed to the container log and is lost with the pod, so a failed run has no diagnostics beyond an exit code. Emit the tail of the log to stderr before `finish`.
findings.scenario: claude exits 1 after an auth error. The work item says `exit=1`, `kubectl logs` shows nothing, and the pod is gone after the TTL.

findings.message: The README says the dispatcher Role can 'never read the namespace's other Secrets'. A holder of `jobs: create` can create a Job that mounts or envFroms any Secret in the namespace (for example `fleet-vault-writer`) and exfiltrate it. Secret `create`-only does not give that guarantee. Soften the claim or document that the dispatcher identity must be trusted.
findings.scenario: A principal with the dispatcher kubeconfig applies a Job whose container has `envFrom: fleet-vault-writer` and prints it to an allowlisted host.
